documents.title: System context: the Document DB platform
documents.plain:
The Document DB platform is one software system. App developers give it schemas and named Effect handlers;
application callers (players and authenticated tenant users) send it HTTP JSON requests; the platform operator
manages tenants, auth, backups and log analysis. The platform publishes snapshots and manifests to object storage,
gives query results and derived event-log rows to an analytics consumer, and takes HTTP load from the k6 load
generator.

Tenant identity comes from API keys, or from headless Better Auth session bearers when enabled. Postgres is part of
the platform and appears on the container view; no external identity provider is wired. No application SQL crosses
the client boundary.

The source was audited against `main` at `643b706` on 2026-10-11 (item 27). FFI-01 to FFI-08 added no actor,
external system or process, so this view is unchanged at the `0b82504` audit stamp.

ste.text:
The Document DB platform is one software system. App developers give schemas and named handlers to the platform.
Application callers send HTTP JSON requests to the platform. The platform operator manages tenants, backups, and log
analysis. The platform sends snapshots and manifests to object storage. The platform gives query results and
event-log rows to the analytics consumer. The k6 load generator sends HTTP load to the platform.

An API key or a Better Auth session identifies the tenant. Postgres is a part of the platform. The platform does not
use an external identity provider. Application SQL does not go across the client boundary.

documents.title: Containers: the request path
documents.plain:
The request path inside the platform: the server process, the DuckDB reader child process, the per-app SQLite files,
the central Postgres registry and the two command-line tools that write to it, with the typed client SDK and object
storage outside.

The writer (server) and the reader remain separate OS processes and native module graphs. Document queries do not go
through the reader: the server opens fresh read-only connections itself, through the FFI SQLite binding over the
system `libsqlite3` (`node:sqlite` is no longer loaded), and authenticated tenant routing selects the file. Unbounded
SQLite reads (any select that is not a primary-key lookup, `count`, `countBy`) run nonblocking under a statement
deadline (default 5 s) and fail with HTTP 504 when it passes; writes and point reads stay blocking (FFI-05). The
DuckDB SQLite extension stays in the separate reader process, so the two SQLite copies never share an address space.
The future control-plane router is not implemented. E2E uses ephemeral Postgres, distinct tenants for layouts, and
fresh Better Auth servers per layout.

The source was audited against `main` at `643b706` (item 27), re-checked for FFI-01 to FFI-05 at `f2bf1c9` and
re-audited at `aa26b27`; FFI-06 to FFI-08 change no element here.

ste.text:
This diagram shows the request path in the platform. The server process receives requests from the typed client SDK.
The server process and the reader process are two different operating-system processes.

The server reads documents itself. It does not send document queries to the reader process. The server opens each
SQLite file through the FFI binding to the system libsqlite3. The tenant of the request selects the file. A read
without a primary-key filter has a deadline. If the deadline passes, the server stops the read and sends HTTP 504.
Writes and point reads do not have a deadline. The reader process keeps the DuckDB SQLite extension. Thus the two
SQLite copies are in different processes.

documents.title: Containers: the observability path
documents.plain:
The observability path: the server and the reader append structured JSONL; the reader ingests it transactionally into
the derived DuckDB event log and then sweeps the safe source files; the logs CLI and the k6 point loader work on the
same stores offline.

Item 23 provides the named catalog and logs CLI; item 25 provides the k6 loader and its join acceptance test. MT-10
wires the reader analysis RPC and shares the ingest instance, so later commits remain visible. The server never opens
DuckDB. Document reads run in-process against application SQLite files; they do not use the reader event-log
database. Retention bounds JSONL only, requires committed watermarks and matching hashes, and never touches today or
the reader sink's open path. Derived tables are never pruned; `logs:compact` remains future work. No load-performance
result is claimed by this diagram.

FFI-06: each `sql` event persists its SQLite execution path (blocking or nonblocking) in the JSONL line and in a
nullable `sql_events.path` column. The `perf/ffi_*.ts` harnesses and the deadline scenario in `tests/integration.ts`
add no container.

ste.text:
This diagram shows the observability path. The server process and the reader process write events to JSONL files.
The reader process ingests the events into the DuckDB event log in one transaction. After the commit, the reader
process compresses or removes the safe JSONL files. The logs CLI can do the same work offline. The k6 point loader
writes k6 measurement points into the event log.

The server process never opens DuckDB. Each sql event records the SQLite execution path: blocking or nonblocking.

documents.title: Components: the server process
documents.plain:
The mounted components of the server process (`PlatformLive`): HTTP and auth, lifecycle, the app and tenant services,
per-app storage, backups, the reader client, in-process document reads, logging, configuration, and the FFI SQLite
binding with its statement classifier. Every storage, document-reader, router and backup open of SQLite goes through
the binding.

Config is acquired before logging, then IdGen, ObjectStore/AppRegistry, TenantRegistry, AppServices and
ReaderClient. Shutdown drains HTTP, stops timers, closes reader and database handles, emits the final lifecycle event,
then drains logging. Every partial startup releases acquired resources. Retention and named analysis execute in the
reader, never as server-side DuckDB components.

The source was audited against `main` at `643b706` (item 27), updated for FFI-01 to FFI-06, and re-audited at
`aa26b27`; FFI-07 and FFI-08 change no element.

ste.text:
This diagram shows the components in the server process. The HTTP component receives each request and identifies the
tenant. The storage component and the document reader open SQLite files through the FFI binding. The statement
classifier selects the execution path of each statement. The logger writes events to JSONL files.

At start, the server gets the configuration first and the logger second. At stop, the server stops HTTP first and
the logger last. The reader process does the event-log analysis. The server process does not use DuckDB.

documents.title: Document DB platform

ste.text:
The platform keeps the documents of each tenant in a SQLite file. It answers authenticated document requests. It
keeps an event log in DuckDB. It sends backups to object storage.

documents.title: Server process
documents.plain:
The writer process: HTTP and auth (Better Auth is mounted at `/api/auth/*`), SQLite document reads and writes, backup
and ingest timers, and the structured logging layer (`LoggingLive`) for HTTP, handler, SQL, transaction and lifecycle
events. Document queries run here on fresh read-only connections opened through the FFI binding; the server never
opens DuckDB. Open the component view for its parts.

ste.text:
The server process is the writer process. It receives HTTP requests and identifies the tenant. It reads and writes
the documents in the SQLite files. It starts the backup timer and the ingest timer. It writes structured events to
JSONL files. It does not open DuckDB.

documents.title: Reader process
documents.plain:
A separate Deno child process that owns the DuckDB event log. It appends reader-role JSONL (stdout is reserved for
RPC), ingests JSONL transactionally and then sweeps safe files, and answers live named-analysis requests on the shared
ingest instance (MT-10), so later commits remain visible. Ingest and analysis handles are independently scoped
connections on that native instance. It keeps the DuckDB SQLite extension, so its SQLite copy never shares an address
space with the server's. Document reads do not use it.

ste.text:
The reader process is a child process of the server. It owns the DuckDB event log. It ingests JSONL events into the
event log. It answers the named analysis requests. It does not read application documents.

documents.title: Application documents
documents.plain:
One SQLite file per tenant at `TENANTS_DIR/tenantId.db`, or the legacy `app.sqlite` under `DATA_DIR` when
`TENANCY=off`. Each app has a `LocalFolderRouter` over the shared tenant directory. Different physical layouts need
distinct tenants, because the schema guard rejects switching layouts. Application documents stay in SQLite.

ste.text:
Each tenant has one SQLite file. The file uses WAL mode. If tenancy is off, the platform uses the legacy file of the
app. The schema guard does not let a tenant change its physical layout.

documents.title: Central registry
documents.plain:
Postgres 17 (`docker-compose.yml`, `platform/tenants/`) holds tenants, hashed keys, users, sessions and memberships.
The server acquires the connection lazily for registry use; `TENANCY=off` preserves app tokens and legacy files.
Better Auth connections are bounded to each request or CLI operation, separate from the lazy registry pool. The
migration runner applies journaled, advisory-locked migrations.

ste.text:
The central registry is a Postgres 17 database. It keeps the tenants, the hashed keys, the users, the sessions, and
the memberships. The server connects to it only when necessary. The migration runner changes its schema.

documents.title: Tenant/auth CLI
documents.plain:
`scripts/tenants.ts` administers tenants and keys; `scripts/auth.ts` is the headless email/password CLI for Better
Auth. Both reach the registry over the Postgres protocol.

ste.text:
The tenant CLI manages tenants and keys. The auth CLI does the auth operations with an email and a password. Both
CLIs connect to the central registry.

documents.title: Structured event sources
documents.plain:
Server and reader JSONL under `LOG_DIR/role/date/events-*.jsonl`; bad lines are quarantined beside their source.
Retention bounds JSONL only: it requires committed watermarks and matching hashes and never touches today's files or
the reader sink's open path. Gzipped retained sources are not re-ingested by the current scanner. Since FFI-06 each
`sql` line carries `path` (blocking or nonblocking). The server component view names the server's own
`LOG_DIR/server/date/` slice of this store "Server JSONL" (inventory decision D2).

ste.text:
The server and the reader write their events to JSONL files. Retention removes only JSONL files. Retention removes a
file only after the ingest commits its events. Retention does not touch the files of the current day.

documents.title: Derived event log
documents.plain:
The derived DuckDB event log (`EVENTLOG_DUCKDB`, schema v2): typed event tables including `sql_events.path`, ingest
watermarks and `k6_points`. Derived tables are never pruned; `logs:compact` remains future work. Ingest runs
`ALTER TABLE sql_events ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS path` on every open, so an older v2 file gains the nullable column on
its next ingest without a schema-version bump; older rows hold NULL. The catalog query
`deadline-hits-per-handler-hour` counts `StatementDeadlineError` sql events by app, handler and UTC hour; until an
older log is re-ingested, that one query fails on the missing column.

ste.text:
The event log is a DuckDB file. It keeps typed events, watermarks, and k6 points. The platform does not delete rows
from the event log. Each ingest adds the path column if the column is missing.

documents.title: Logs CLI
documents.plain:
`scripts/logs.ts`: ingest, list, query and sweep, with the named analysis catalog. The standalone CLI queries
read-only and can fail while a writer owns the DuckDB file; use the live admin route while the server runs. Its sweep
in dry-run mode only plans.

ste.text:
The logs CLI ingests, lists, queries, and sweeps the event log offline. A query from the CLI can fail while the
reader process writes to the file. While the server operates, use the admin route.

documents.title: k6 point loader
documents.plain:
`perf/ingest_k6.ts` (item 25) reads `raw.json` of a selected k6 run from `logs/k6/run-id/` and inserts its raw metric
points into `k6_points`; a catalog query compares overlapping HTTP buckets. Item 25 also adds the join acceptance
test. No load-performance result is claimed by this view.

ste.text:
The k6 point loader reads the raw points of one k6 run. It writes the points into the event log. A catalog query
compares the k6 points with the HTTP events.

documents.title: HTTP API / auth
documents.plain:
`platform/http/`, `platform/auth/` and `core/errors.ts`: named routes, traces, and tenant, API-key and session
authentication. Auth derives `TenantContext` before consuming app arguments. HTTP status mapping lives in
`core/errors.ts`: `toHttpStatus` maps `StatementDeadlineError` to 504. Better Auth connections are bounded to each
request, separate from the lazy registry pool.

ste.text:
The HTTP component receives each request. It identifies the tenant before it reads the arguments of the app. It
sends HTTP 504 when a statement deadline passes.

documents.title: Server lifecycle
documents.plain:
`platform/server.ts`: the scoped listener, the backup and hourly ingest timers, and the reader-exit watch. Startup
acquires Config before logging, then IdGen, ObjectStore/AppRegistry, TenantRegistry, AppServices and ReaderClient.
Shutdown drains HTTP, stops timers, closes reader and database handles, emits the final lifecycle event, then drains
logging. Every partial startup releases the resources it acquired.

ste.text:
The lifecycle component starts and stops the server. At start, it gets the configuration before the logger. At stop,
it stops HTTP first. Then it stops the timers and closes the reader and the database handles. It stops the logger
last.

documents.title: AppRegistry / AppServices
documents.plain:
`platform/registry.ts` and `platform/layers.ts`: app schemas and named handlers, and a Storage and Backups stack per
app. Startup loads `libsqlite3` once and logs a `lifecycle` event, phase `sqlite-library`, with the resolved path and
version. Item 26 removed the compatibility wrappers and `platform/compiler.ts`; pure compilation lives in
`core/compile/` and adds no runtime component.

ste.text:
The app registry keeps the schema and the named handlers of each app. It makes one storage service and one backup
service for each app. At start, it loads the SQLite library one time.

documents.title: TenantRegistry
documents.plain:
`platform/tenants/store.ts`: the lazily opened Postgres registry with a bounded, TTL-limited cache of hashed keys.
Tenant key revocation invalidates the local cache; other instances converge within the cache TTL.

ste.text:
The tenant registry reads tenants and hashed keys from Postgres. It keeps a cache of the hashed keys. When an operator
revokes a key, the local cache removes it. Other server instances remove it when its cache time ends.

documents.title: TenantStorageRouter
documents.plain:
`platform/tenants/routing.ts`: a `LocalFolderRouter` per app over validated tenant locations. It opens and prepares
the tenant SQLite file through the FFI binding and runs the schema guard. The tenant location is prepared behind a
shared initialization barrier.

ste.text:
The storage router finds the SQLite file of the tenant. It prepares the file one time through the FFI binding. It
checks the schema of the file.

documents.title: TenantContext
documents.plain:
A request-local service that holds the trusted, credential-derived tenant id and scopes the rest of the request.
Storage resolves the tenant's writer from it and never from caller-supplied selectors.

ste.text:
The tenant context keeps the tenant id of one request. The tenant id comes from the credential. The storage component
uses only this tenant id. The caller cannot select the tenant.

documents.title: Storage
documents.plain:
`platform/sqlite.ts`: scoped writer handles, serialized mutations, rollback and context expiry. Tenant-mode writers
use a bounded, scope-owned handle cache (default 64 handles, 60-second idle expiry); requests lease handles, and
shutdown drains leases before closing them. Writes and point reads run blocking on the main thread; unbounded reads run
`allAsync`/`getAsync` under the statement deadline. A per-connection `ConnectionGate`, shared with the document
reader, keeps one statement at a time on a connection. A step that has not returned `statementInterruptGraceMs`
after its interrupt poisons the connection: an error-level lifecycle event, no further statements, and the connection
closes when the step returns.

ste.text:
The storage component writes the documents of a tenant. It does each mutation in a serialized transaction. It keeps
a cache of writer handles. Writes and point reads use the blocking path. Other reads use the nonblocking path and
have a deadline. One connection executes one statement at a time. If a statement does not stop after the interrupt,
the component closes the connection.

documents.title: Backups / ObjectStore
documents.plain:
`platform/backup.ts` and `platform/object_store.ts`: snapshot, hash and manifest, published to local files or signed
S3. Storage provides a consistent `VACUUM INTO` snapshot; the backup verifier opens the copy read-only through the
FFI binding and runs `quick_check` before publication. The lifecycle component owns the scoped backup timer.

ste.text:
The backup component makes a snapshot of each SQLite file. It checks the snapshot copy before it publishes the copy.
It publishes the snapshot and a manifest to object storage.

documents.title: ReaderClient / ReaderProcess
documents.plain:
`platform/ipc.ts` and `platform/layers.ts`: the scoped reader child for ingest and analysis, with a capped queue, a
call deadline and trace propagation. Retention and named analysis execute in the reader, never as server-side DuckDB
components. The call-level `reader.callTimeoutMs` guard stays; config validation keeps the statement deadline below
it, so the statement deadline fires first.

ste.text:
The reader client starts the reader process and sends requests to it. It sends ingest and analysis requests over
JSONL IPC. It stops the reader process when the server stops.

documents.title: DocumentReaderClient
documents.plain:
`platform/document_reader.ts`: document queries run in-process on a read-only connection, with a concurrency cap of
32 and the shared `ConnectionGate`. Point reads run blocking; every other select runs `allAsync` under
`sqlite.statementDeadlineMs` and fails `StatementDeadlineError` (HTTP 504) when the deadline passes. Document reads
do not go through the reader child or DuckDB.

ste.text:
The document reader executes the document queries in the server process. It uses a read-only connection. It executes
a maximum of 32 queries at the same time. A point read uses the blocking path. Other queries use the nonblocking path
and have a deadline.

documents.title: FFI SQLite binding
documents.plain:
`platform/sqlite_ffi/`: the system `libsqlite3` through `Deno.dlopen`. Since FFI-04 every server SQLite open goes
through it on `Config.sqlite.library`, and `node:sqlite` is not in the server runtime graph
(`tests/unit/boundaries_test.ts`). FFI-04b: every open, read-only included, applies `node:sqlite`-compatible defaults
(double-quoted string literals off, `foreign_keys` on) before any caller SQL, and loading refuses darwin/aarch64.
FFI-05: blocking `sqlite3_step` on the main thread for writes and point reads; a nonblocking path (`allAsync`/
`getAsync` on Deno's blocking pool) for unbounded reads, where the binding calls `sqlite3_interrupt` at the deadline.
It keeps a 64-statement cache.

ste.text:
The FFI binding loads the system SQLite library. Each SQLite open in the server uses the binding. The binding has a
blocking path and a nonblocking path. The blocking path executes on the main thread. The nonblocking path executes on
a pool thread. At the deadline, the binding interrupts the statement.

documents.title: Statement classifier
documents.plain:
`platform/sqlite_ffi/classify.ts`: `classify(operation)` works from the plan IR, never from SQL text. `insert`,
`patch`, `delete` and a select with `_id` equality and no aggregate are bounded and take the blocking path; every
other select, `count` and `countBy` is unbounded and takes the nonblocking path. Writes never take the nonblocking
path: an interrupt landing after an async write committed would leave the commit standing while the caller saw a
failure.

ste.text:
The statement classifier reads the plan of each operation. It does not read the SQL text. A write or a point read is
bounded. A bounded operation uses the blocking path. All other reads are unbounded. An unbounded read uses the
nonblocking path.

documents.title: Logger / EventSink
documents.plain:
`platform/logging/`: the Effect logger and event sink, with a dropping queue, batched JSONL appends, rotation and a
final drain when its scope closes. Every `sql` event carries `path` (blocking or nonblocking); since FFI-06 it is
written to the JSONL line. A stuck statement is reported as an ordinary error-level `lifecycle` event.

ste.text:
The logger receives events from the other components. It puts the events in a queue. If the queue is full, the
logger discards the new events. It writes the events to JSONL files in batches. When the server stops, the logger
writes all the events in the queue.

documents.title: Config / IdGen
documents.plain:
`platform/config.ts` and `platform/sqlite.ts`: validated options, UUIDs and the clock. All three SQLite options are
read: `sqlite.library` (the `libsqlite3` path passed to every open), `sqlite.statementDeadlineMs` and
`sqlite.statementInterruptGraceMs`. Validation keeps the statement deadline below `reader.callTimeoutMs`.

ste.text:
The config component reads and validates the options. It gives the SQLite library path to the FFI binding. It gives
the statement deadline and the interrupt grace period to the storage component and the document reader.
